n: Writing on September 6, 1842, while still in hiding, Joseph returns to baptism for the dead—the subject weighing most on his mind.

f.w: press itself upon my feelings the strongest
f.g: Joseph felt deep urgency about the salvation of the dead.

n: He recalls his earlier instruction that a recorder must witness each baptism with his own eyes and ears.

f.w: a recorder, who should be eye-witness

n: Since one recorder can’t attend everything, each ward of Nauvoo should have its own careful recorder, noting dates, names, and details, plus about three witnesses—following the biblical rule of two or three witnesses.

f.w: in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established

f.g: In Nauvoo, a civic division of the city; the term later became the Church’s local congregation.

n: Ward records then go to a general Church recorder, who enters them in the general record with the certificates. Done properly, this is as valid as if he had witnessed them himself.
This may seem detailed, but it follows an order God established before the world for saving those who died without the gospel.

f.w: die without a knowledge of the gospel

n: Joseph quotes John’s vision of the dead being judged from the books, including the book of life.
Joseph interprets: “the books” are earthly records of what was done; “the book of life” is heaven’s record. Earth’s records and heaven’s records correspond.
This ordinance depends on priesthood power to bind and loose. Put another way: what is recorded on earth is recorded in heaven. People are judged by ordinances done personally or by proxy.

f.g: Latin, “in one’s own person”—personally rather than by proxy.

f.w: by the means of their own agents
f.g: Through proxies who stand in for them.

n: This may sound bold, but whenever God gave a dispensation of priesthood, this power came with it. Ordinances done with authority and faithfully recorded become binding in heaven.

f.w: This is a faithful saying. Who can hear it?

n: As precedent, Joseph quotes Jesus giving Peter the keys of the kingdom and the power to bind and loose.
The key to it all—the “summum bonum”—is gaining the powers of the holy priesthood. With those keys, knowledge about saving the living and the dead follows.
Baptism by immersion represents death and resurrection: going down into the water like burial, coming up like rising from the grave. This symbolism ties naturally to baptism for the dead.

f.w: in the likeness of the resurrection

n: So the baptismal font represents the grave and is placed below where the living gather. Temple fonts are still located on a lower level, often resting on twelve oxen.
Quoting Paul: the natural comes first, then the spiritual. As earthly records are faithfully kept, so heaven’s records are kept. This is the sealing power and, in one sense, the “key of knowledge.”

f.w: The first man is of the earth, earthy

n: One of the great principles of family history: our ancestors’ salvation is necessary to ours. As Paul taught, they cannot be made perfect without us—nor we without them.

f.w: they without us cannot be made perfect

n: Joseph cites Paul’s mention of people being baptized for the dead as evidence the practice existed anciently.
He quotes Malachi’s prophecy of Elijah turning hearts of fathers and children toward each other, calling baptism for the dead “this most glorious of all subjects.”

f.w: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet

n: Joseph explains: there must be a “welding link” between generations—baptism for the dead and sealing. All dispensations, keys, and glories since Adam will be welded together, and hidden truths revealed to the humble.

f.g: A strong bond fusing two parts into one.

n: Joseph bursts into joy: the gospel is a voice of gladness, mercy, and truth for the living and the dead. He quotes Isaiah’s “how beautiful upon the mountains.”

f.w: a voice of truth out of the earth

f.g: Mount Carmel in Israel was known for heavy, refreshing dew and fertility.

n: He recounts the Restoration: Moroni at Cumorah, the Three Witnesses at Fayette, Michael exposing the devil on the Susquehanna, and Peter, James, and John restoring keys in the wilderness between Harmony and Colesville.

f.w: The voice of Peter, James, and John

n: God spoke in Peter Whitmer Sr.’s home in Fayette and in many places since. Angels—Michael (Adam), Gabriel, Raphael, and others—restored their keys “line upon line.”

f.w: the chamber of old Father Whitmer
f.g: The Church was organized in the Peter Whitmer Sr. home on April 6, 1830.
An angel named in Jewish tradition; his specific role in the Restoration is not otherwise explained.

f.w: line upon line, precept upon precept

n: A rousing call: go forward, not backward! Courage! Let even the dead praise Christ, who ordained a way to free them from their spirit prison.

f.g: Hebrew “God with us,” a title of Christ.

n: All creation is invited to rejoice—mountains, seas, rivers, trees, rocks, sun, moon, and stars—echoing the morning stars singing at creation.
Quoting Malachi on the Lord as a refiner, Joseph urges the Saints to offer an “offering in righteousness”: a book of their dead’s records presented in the finished temple.

f.w: like a refiner's fire, and like fuller's soap

f.g: A strong cleaning agent used to whiten cloth.

f.w: a book containing the records of our dead

n: Joseph closes warmly, promising more on the subject, as their humble servant and steadfast friend.

f.g: A friend who never turns aside or wavers.
